01

The Leverage Point

ICP is step 1 of a five-part loop — and it's the part that decides everything after it. The order is ICP → Offer & Lead Magnet → Campaign Architecture → Copy → Lead List Building. Your ICP decides which offer and lead magnet you need, which decides which campaigns you run, which decides the copy you write, which decides the data you have to go find when you build the list.

Most people treat these as five separate jobs. They're one loop. This doc is where the loop starts — so the decisions you make here ripple through all four docs after it. Take your time on it.

Most people who fail at cold outbound fail here, not at copy. They write decent emails to the wrong people, get terrible reply rates, and decide the channel is dead. The channel was never the problem. They were broadcasting into the wrong room.

“

Think of it like baking. Copy is the icing. The offer is the filling. The ICP is the ingredients themselves. You can't decorate your way out of bad batter.

We've watched a SaaS company doing $20M selling to "any mid-market business" — spread across a dozen industries, growing slowly, decent everywhere and special nowhere. They went all-in on one vertical and scaled past $150M. Same product. Same team. Same playbook. They just stopped talking to everyone and started talking to someone. That's the leverage.

02

ICP vs Buyer Persona

These get blended constantly. They are not the same thing.

The company

ICP

The Ideal Customer Profile — the company you target. “B2B SaaS, 100–500 employees, $10–50M ARR, US/UK, running HubSpot.”

The person

Buyer persona

The person inside that company — the VP of Sales, the Head of RevOps, the CRO. One ICP can have several personas.

If you sell sales-enablement software, the ICP is one company type, but your personas might be the CRO (economic buyer), the Head of Sales Ops (technical buyer), and the VP of Sales (the user). Each one hears a different message.

The rule for outbound: one persona per campaign. Don't blend. The CRO and the Head of Sales Ops have different concerns, language, and objections. Copy that tries to speak to both speaks to neither. Separate campaigns — exactly how is covered in Campaign Architecture (SOP 08).

03

The 4-Layer ICP Framework

Every good ICP has four layers stacked. Build top to bottom — each layer narrows the one above it.

1
Firmographics — the company basics

The objective facts. What is measurable from the outside. Look at your top 10–20 customers — highest LTV, fastest close, lowest churn — and see what they cluster around.

Criteria
Example

B2B SaaS, e-commerce, professional services, healthcare
Company size
50–500 employees

$10M–$50M ARR
Location
US-based, expanding to EU
Company age
3–10 years — past early stage, pre-enterprise
Business model
B2B vs B2C vs B2B2C
Funding stage
Bootstrapped, Seed, Series A–C, PE-backed
2
Technographics — the tools they run

What software they already use reveals budget, sophistication, and intent. A company running Salesforce plus a sales-engagement tool is signaling sales maturity and an active outbound motion; a company with none of that gets a different message entirely. Tools like BuiltWith, Clearbit, or HG Insights expose tech-stack data that filters cleanly inside your enrichment workflow.

Signal type
Example tools
CRM
Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive
Marketing automation
Marketo, Pardot, ActiveCampaign, Shopify
Sales tools
Outreach, Salesloft, the existing outbound stack
Analytics
Segment, Amplitude, Mixpanel
Competitor tools
Companies on your competitors' tools are ripe for switching
Complementary tools
Companies on tools that integrate with yours adopt faster
3
Buying signals — what's happening right now

The behavioral layer, and the one most people under-build. A trigger is a specific event that makes a prospect more buyable today than yesterday. This is where you find not just who fits, but who is ready. Triggers fall into three categories.

Individual
  • New role, or first time in a role of this level — gold, since vendor changes happen in the first 90 days.
  • Promoted recently; hiring on their team.
  • Posting, commenting, or following relevant content; spoke on a podcast or at an event — a public POV you can reference.
  • Attending an event; joined a relevant community.
Company
  • Open jobs or hiring posts — active need + budget. A role that doesn't exist is a pitch angle of its own (no CFO → pitch fractional; no Head of RevOps → pitch your tool).
  • Recently raised funding (vendor-shopping mode); new tech installed (adoption window for adjacent tools).
  • Decision-maker departure (vendor relationships in flux); layoffs or headcount cuts (cost-cutting mode — an opportunity if you reduce cost).
  • Legal issues or lawsuits (compliance, security, risk tooling); negative employee reviews; website redesign or migration.
  • Using a competitor, or a tool you integrate with (switching opportunity); a customer lookalike.
  • SEC filings / annual reports; expansion, new office, or new market; M&A; partnerships; product launches; a competitor's launch in their space.
Industry
  • Trends (AI adoption, cost pressure), analyst reports that mention your category, new regulation, and world events. Industry triggers rarely carry an email alone — they make an individual or company trigger feel urgent, the macro framing around the specific reason you're reaching out.
4
Psychographics — what they value

The softest layer. Hardest to pull from a database, most powerful when you nail it. Read their About page, careers page, and blog. Skim the CEO's LinkedIn. Use AI to summarize values from their site at scale.

Indicator
What it tells you & how to find it
Growth vs optimization mode
Different urgency, different language — read via hiring velocity and leadership messaging.
Data-driven culture
Decision style — use of analytics tools, data-team size.
Customer-centric
Operating priority — NPS, CS team size, reviews.
Compliance-focused
Risk tolerance — industry regulations, certifications.
Remote vs office-first
Operating model — job postings, culture pages.

04

The Signal-to-Offer Map

Here's the move that ties this whole playbook together, and it's the thing most operators miss. Every offer has a specific set of public, findable data points that prove a prospect has the exact pain you solve — right now. Those same data points do two jobs at once: they score the lead, and they write the personalization. One enrichment, two jobs — that's what keeps your list costs sane (more on that in Lead List Building).

Real-world examples

A compliance SaaS reaching a company that just got named in an FTC action or disclosed a breach. The lawsuit is the pain. "Saw the FTC filing last month — figured compliance gaps are top of mind" both scores the lead A-tier and writes the opener.

A building-materials supplier reaching a developer who just filed a construction permit or won a bid — the permit is the buying window. A staffing firm reaching a company that just posted ten roles in one department.

Ask one question for your offer: what public event means this prospect has my pain today? That event becomes both your filter and your first line.

05

Two Campaign Motions from One ICP

Your ICP work produces two distinct lists — and they become two distinct campaign types. You decide the split here; you build the structure in Campaign Architecture.

Broad · scalable

Evergreen cash-cow list

Everyone who fits your ICP on firmographics, regardless of signal. Copy has to work cold because there's no signal to lean on. Lower conversion per email, but it runs forever and pays the bills. This is your baseline pipeline.

Smaller · higher-converting

Signal list

The subset showing one or more Signal-to-Offer triggers. More expensive to build (more enrichment), but far higher conversion. Earns hyper-personalized copy and multi-touch outreach (email + LinkedIn + a call) because the economics justify the effort.

You run both. The cash cow funds the operation; the signal list spikes your conversion rate. Don't pick one — hand both forward to Campaign Architecture (SOP 08).

06

Build Your ICP — The 30-Minute Exercise

Stop guessing. Use real data.

  1. Pull your top 10% of customers — highest LTV, fastest close, lowest churn, easiest to work with, most excited about your product.
  2. Find 3 patterns they share: industry, size, revenue band, tech stack, funding stage, geography.
  3. Pull your bottom 5 customers — churned fast, slow close, high support load, painful.
  4. Find 2 patterns they share. This is your anti-ICP — companies to avoid even when they look good on paper.
  5. Write your ICP in one paragraph. Example: “B2B SaaS, 100–500 employees, $10–50M ARR, Series A–B, US/UK, running Salesforce and a sales-engagement tool, recently raised OR hiring for RevOps, with a data-driven culture.”
  6. Build the scoring rubric (next section).

A list without a score treats every lead as equal. They aren't. Score every company 0–100 against your rubric, then tier them — the tier decides the treatment, which is the part most people skip.

08

Positioning: Niching & Ocean State

Two levels of niching

Campaign-level niching is mandatory. Each campaign targets one ICP segment and one persona — never blend mid-market e-commerce with enterprise SaaS in one campaign; the messaging dilutes and the data becomes unreadable. Brand-level niching is optional, and eventually right once you have the case studies to dominate one space. The usual right move: niche at the campaign level from day one, niche at the brand level once you have the proof to own it.

The hourglass

Most successful B2B companies follow an hourglass across their life: early — experiment broadly to find a niche you can win; growth — go all-in where the experiments worked, this is where revenue compounds; scale — expand into adjacent niches once you've dominated the first. If you're early, don't get stuck broad. Pick a niche, prove it, expand.

Red ocean vs blue ocean

Once you have an ICP, ask how saturated the market is — it decides how much creative work your offer and copy have to do. Red ocean — every prospect gets 30 cold emails a week in your category, and competitors 2–3x your size do roughly what you do. Generic value props die here; you need a creative offer, a specific mechanism, sharp differentiation, and strong risk reversal. Blue ocean — few competitors emailing them, problems unsolved. Direct wins: three-sentence emails, a plain "we do X for Y without Z," fast conversion because you're often their first option.

Real-world example

A B2B affordable-housing certification software targeting Section 8 housing found a true blue ocean — most prospects had never been emailed about the problem. Three sentences per email, direct value prop — the niche was so underserved that complexity would have hurt.

20%

ICP isn't just who — it's what market state you're in. That tells you immediately how hard the offer and copy have to work.

09

Pain Research — The Core Diagnostic

Before anyone writes copy, you have to understand the pain from the prospect's point of view. Answer these for every ICP:

  1. What pain do they actually face? Not what your product solves — what they wake up worried about.
  2. What are they doing about it now? Workarounds, competitors, or just living with it.
  3. What is the pain costing them? Dollars, time, risk, missed opportunity.
  4. Why is their current fix broken — and worse than yours?
  5. What do they want instead? The end state they picture if it went away.
  6. What emotional and logical win can you deliver, better than anything else on the market?

Answer these and your offer and copy practically write themselves. Skip them and you'll write generic copy because you don't actually know what the prospect cares about. How to research it fast: read Reddit threads in their industry, G2 reviews of competitors, LinkedIn posts from people in that role. Listen to podcast episodes with that persona. Have 5 real conversations — or have Claude do the reading and surface the pattern.

10

Common ICP Mistakes

Avoid these
  • ✕Too broad. "Any company with 10+ employees." You can't market to everyone. Specificity wins.
  • ✕Too narrow. "Fintech in SF with exactly 150 employees." TAM too small to sustain pipeline — fine for a one-off, not for pipeline.
  • ✕Built on assumptions, not data. Talk to customers, look at your CRM, don't guess.
  • ✕Static. Markets move. Re-run this quarterly.
  • ✕Ignoring the anti-ICP. Knowing who NOT to target is as valuable as knowing who to.
  • ✕No scoring. Without it, every lead looks equal. Score them.
  • ✕Treating signals as a separate, later step. The triggers and the Signal-to-Offer Map are part of defining the ICP — do them here, not as an afterthought when you're building the list.
Action items
  • Pull your top 10 customers; find 3 shared patterns. Pull your bottom 5; find 2 anti-patterns.
  • Write your ICP in one paragraph using the 4 layers.
  • List the individual / company / industry triggers that matter for your offer.
  • Build your Signal-to-Offer Map: name the public events that mean a prospect has your pain right now.
  • Decide red ocean or blue ocean — it sets how creative the offer and copy need to be.
  • Answer the 6 pain-research questions (use our Claude skill to speed it up).
  • Build the 0–100 scoring rubric and decide what each tier gets.
  • Split your ICP into the two campaign motions: evergreen cash cow + signal list.
